brief.text:
You're inside. Good. Now the money.

Their storefront's got a search box — type a product, it hands you back rows. Looks harmless. But that search and the account ledgers drink from the same well.

Ask it for a product and it answers polite. Ask it for a product and the ledger in the same breath — and it hands you both. Long as you match the shape it expects. Pull me the vault.
brief.objective: Pull a hidden account off a shopping page.

debrief.explanation: The search term is concatenated into the LIKE pattern, so a closing quote ends the search string and lets you append UNION SELECT. UNION staples a second query - from an unrelated table - onto the same result set; the only requirement is a matching column count, which is why the recon step is discovering that the query returns 3 columns.

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - the search term is interpolated into the LIKE pattern
cur.execute(
    f"SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{q}%'"
)
rows = cur.fetchall()
# Concatenation is the same flaw: "... LIKE '%" + q + "%'"

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: PHP (PDO)
Java (JDBC)
C# / .NET (ADO.NET)
Go (database/sql)
Ruby on Rails (ActiveRecord)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - the search term is interpolated into the LIKE pattern
rows = Product.where(
  "name LIKE '%#{q}%'"
)
# find_by_sql is just as unsafe: Product.find_by_sql("... LIKE '%#{q}%'")

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: Laravel (Query Builder)
Django (ORM)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - input interpolated into raw SQL, bypassing the ORM's binding
rows = Product.objects.raw(
    f"SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{q}%'"
)
# .extra(where=[f"name LIKE '%{q}%'"]) is just as unsafe

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: Spring Boot (JdbcTemplate)

secureCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
secureCodeVariants.code:
# sqlite3 — the % wildcards belong to the bound value, not the SQL
cur.execute(
    "SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE ?",
    (f"%{q}%",),
)
rows = cur.fetchall()
# psycopg2 uses %s: cur.execute("... WHERE name LIKE %s", (f"%{q}%",))

secureCodeVariants.label: PHP (PDO)
Java (JDBC)
C# / .NET (ADO.NET)
Go (database/sql)
Ruby on Rails (ActiveRecord)
secureCodeVariants.code:
# ActiveRecord — the % wildcards are part of the bound value, not the SQL
rows = Product.where(
  "name LIKE ?", "%#{q}%"
)
# Named form: Product.where("name LIKE :p", p: "%#{q}%")

secureCodeVariants.label: Laravel (Query Builder)
Django (ORM)
secureCodeVariants.code:
# Django ORM — __contains binds the term as a parameter (never raw SQL)
rows = Product.objects.filter(
    name__contains=q
)
# Explicit .raw(): Product.objects.raw("... WHERE name LIKE %s", ["%" + q + "%"])

secureCodeVariants.label: Spring Boot (JdbcTemplate)

debrief.takeaway: If the query's shape can't change, no second question rides in on it.

database.schemaSql: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, price REAL); CREATE TABLE offshore_accounts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, holder_name TEXT, account_ref TEXT, balance_usd INTEGER);

winCondition.reason: Vault manifest surfaced in the result grid - the cross-table UNION held.

hints.text: The search only knows how to hand back one shape of answer. Learn that shape first — how wide it is — then a second question can ride out on the same tray.
First find how many columns come back: ORDER BY 1, 2, 3 ... until it breaks; the last one that works is the count. Then UNION SELECT that many values - the second query must match the column count.
It is 3 columns. Try  ' UNION SELECT holder_name, account_ref, balance_usd FROM offshore_accounts --

inputs.q: ' UNION SELECT holder_name, account_ref, balance_usd FROM offshore_accounts --

expectedSolution.note: First the column count:  ' ORDER BY 3 --   is OK,  ' ORDER BY 4 --   errors => 3 columns.
